the optimal memory of an organization is that which allows it to be as flexible as possible in a given environment, while being robust to the changes that are expected to occur.
the optimal amount of memory is zero, but only in simple and stable worlds.

(1) the more complex and non-stationary the environment, the more important is the memory, but (2) there is some critical complexity threshold beyond which the memory does not matter any more, (3) the memory should be robust to changes, and (4) the more complex the environment, the less robust the memory needs to be.

the interplay between memory, complexity and non-staionarity, and its consequences for organizational learning and adaptation.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
memory matters for performance, provided that the environment is sufficiently complex.
memory matters in complex, non-stationary environments, but only up to a point.

the optimal memory of organizations depends on the complexity and stability of the environment, but that the best strategy in the long run is to have a memory that is sufficiently flexible to be able to forget.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolutionary dynamics of organizations in complex and dynamic worlds is not necessarily a race to the bottom of forgetfulness and myopia.
